en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-Ānanda-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Shi Fajian.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "There are those who serve the Buddha and obtain wealth, status, and favorable benefits; there are also those who suffer decline."
"If they are dissimilar in their exhaustion, why are they not equal?
We pray that the God among Gods will explain this for us all.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"There are those who revere the Buddha, receive the precepts from an enlightened teacher, maintain single-minded faith without transgression, and practice with diligence, never failing in what they have received.
They keep the images bright and clean, performing prostrations morning and evening, and reverently lighting lamps."

Abiding in pure giving, they do not violate the prohibitions of the Way; never wearying of the fasts and precepts, their hearts are filled with joy. They are constantly protected by the various devas and benevolent spirits;
whatever they undertake meets with success, and all their undertakings increase twofold. Respected by devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and the masses, they will surely attain Buddhahood in the future.
These are the true disciples of the Buddha among good sons and good daughters.
"There are those who serve the Buddha but do not encounter a virtuous teacher, nor do they see the scriptural teachings; they merely receive the precepts."
They merely display the names of precepts while remaining muddled and lacking faith; they violate the monastic rules, wavering between belief and disbelief with a hesitant mind.
Furthermore, they possess neither scriptures nor images; they do not daily burn incense or perform prostrations, and they constantly harbor anger and resentment.
They utter harsh words and abuse others, do not observe the six fast days, and kill living beings with their own hands.
They show no respect for the Buddhist scriptures, storing them in worn-out chests or keeping them upon the beds of their wives and children.
Or perhaps it is hung on a wall without any intention of providing a seat for its veneration; in this, it is no different from the ordinary books of the world.

If one who is ill harbors doubts and lacks faith, they will instead summon shamans to perform divinations and offerings to heterodox deities. Consequently, the celestial deities will distance themselves and fail to provide protection, while demons and specters advance daily and evil spirits mass at the gate. This causes one's resources to decline and whatever they undertake to fail.
Those who commit sins in the present life are not disciples of the Buddha; upon death, they shall enter the hells (*niraya*) and be subjected to interrogation, punishment, and torture.

Because of their offenses, they experience decline and ruin in the present life and will further suffer calamities thereafter; when their souls depart at death, the agony is so extreme that it is beyond description.

"Fools are utterly blind; they do not contemplate the causal conditions of their past lives, nor where their spirits have been directed, nor their fundamental origins. They claim that serving the Buddha has brought about this decline and ruin."
They feel no shame for their lack of merit in past lives, blaming the sages and accusing Heaven; such is the delusion and confusion of worldly people, failing to understand to this extent.

These ignorant ones are full of doubt and hesitation, their faith is not firm, and their minds are unsettled. They lose the proper way in both advancing and retreating, betraying the Buddha’s grace without any sense of gratitude, and consequently become entangled and bound by the three miserable realms, creating their own fortune and calamity.

The conditions for sinful consciousness take root in their origins; one must not fail to accord with this. The ten evils are enemies, while the ten virtues are steadfast friends. To settle the spirit and attain the Way—all arises from goodness.

Virtue is a great armor; one who does not fear the sword and spear, who is able to maintain faithfulness, and whose household is harmonious and peaceful, will naturally receive blessings—not because they are bestowed by a deity.
"If they do not believe now, their suffering in future lives will become even more severe!
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda!..."
Good and evil follow a person like a shadow follows a form; they cannot be separated.
The matters of sin and merit are likewise so; do not harbor doubts, lest you fall into the evil realms!
"Believe with certainty and do not be deluded; wherever you are, you shall always be at peace. The Buddha’s words are most sincere and never deceive anyone.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda: "The Buddha does not speak with duplicity. The sutras and Dharma are difficult to hear.

You possess merit from past lives and have now been able to attend upon the Buddha. You should remember to repay this kindness by disseminating the teachings of the Dharma and manifesting them to the people, acting as a field of merit for them. Those who believe shall encounter [the Dharma], and in future lives they will have no sorrow."
Ānanda received the instruction and respectfully promulgated it everywhere.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a person does not kill with their own hand but instructs another to kill, is there no offense for one who does not kill with their own hand?"
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! To instruct another to kill is more grave than to kill oneself."
Why is this? It may be that they are slaves, servants, or lowly persons who do not understand the laws regarding offenses;

or they may have been coerced by local officials into performing service against their will. Although they incur punishment, because their intent differs from that of the instigator, there is a distinction in the gravity of the offense.

To instruct others in killing is to knowingly and intentionally commit an offense; to harbor secret thoughts of malice and harm, to act with the hands of a foolish evildoer, and to lack a heart of compassion;
to deceive the Triple Gem and likewise naturally commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), harming living beings and truncating their lives—there is no sin greater than this!
When enemies retaliate against one another, they suffer calamities life after life; as they pass from one to another in mutual retribution, there is no end to it.

They find no peace in the present life and frequently encounter misfortune and disaster. Upon death, they enter hell; once they emerge from their human form, they shall fall among the animals, where they will be butchered by humans. For billions of kalpas across the three miserable realms and eight difficulties, they shall provide their flesh to others, with no time of cessation in sight.

They cause their bodies to suffer hardship, eating grass and drinking from springs; such beasts and animals exist visibly in the present world because, in previous lives when they were humans, they were violent, rebellious, and unprincipled, secretly harming and injuring living beings. It is due to a lack of faith that they have reached this state; life after life they act as enemies, returning to repay one another. Though their spirits are the same, their forms differ; the depth of their transgressions is thus.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Worldly people and the disciples of the Buddha who harbor evil intentions toward their teachers or those of virtuous character—what is their transgression?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"As for those who are human, they should love and delight in the goodness of others, taking the virtuous as their friends and not envying them.
If a person harbors ill will toward one who possesses virtue or toward a good teacher, this is no different from harboring ill will toward the Buddha."
"It would be better to take up a ten-thousand-stone crossbow and turn it upon one's own body.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Would it not be painful to shoot one's own body?"
Ānanda said:
"It is most painful, most painful!
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
“If a person harbors an evil intent toward one who possesses the Way and its Virtue, or toward their teacher, the pain is more severe than being struck by a crossbow bolt in the body.

As a disciple, one must not treat one’s teacher with contempt or harbor ill will toward those who possess the Way and its Virtue; one should regard them as if they were the Buddha and must not envy their goodness.”
Those who possess the virtue of precepts move all the devas; among devas, nāgas, and spirits, there are none who do not revere them.
It would be better to cast oneself into fire or have one's flesh cut by a sharp blade than to harbor jealousy toward the goodness of others; such a transgression is no small matter.
"Be careful!
Be careful! Ānanda said.
"Is it not the case that what the teacher does may be clearly wrong for the disciple?
Can a minor offense not become a major one?
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted!
It is indeed most profound and most profound!
The principle between teacher and disciple is naturally moved by righteousness; only after one has granted their consent should they regard the other as themselves."
"Do not impose upon others what you do not desire for yourself; uphold and honor the codes of propriety and law so as not to allow resentment or litigation, and let your disciples do likewise.

Let both teacher and disciple be sincere in these two principles: the teacher should act as a true teacher, and the disciple should act as a true disciple. Do not slander one another; be careful not to harbor malice, for a small grudge can grow into a great one and burn oneself."

I observe that in the final age, there will be multitudes of evil people—bhikṣus of the demonic world—who think only of the faults of others while failing to restrain their own evils. Envious of the worthy and jealous of the virtuous, they do not contemplate the practice of the Path; being unable to practice it themselves, they further disparage and destroy others, severing their resolve for the Path and preventing them from practicing.

To be greedy for worldly affairs and lose oneself in the accumulation of wealth is to fall into the great hells of evil retribution after death; one ought not to be thus. What is there to seek in this world?

One should mindfully entrust oneself to the grace of the Buddha and lead one another by means of the Way. The Way must be studied, for it delivers the spirit from suffering and enables transcendence of birth and death. When you see the worthy, do not treat them with arrogance; when you see the good, do not slander them. Do not take a minor transgression as proof of a person’s great crime. To violate the law and lose the principle of truth is a sin of no small magnitude.
"Since there is evidence for both sin and merit, how can one not be cautious!
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the circumstances of managing a household for disciples in the final age, what should they do according to the practical requirements of each situation?"
The Buddha said:
"Having received the prohibitory precepts of the Buddha, one should believe in and practice them, not harboring deceit or falsehood, but honoring filial piety and maintaining reverent caution!
By reverently taking refuge in the Triple Gem, supporting one's parents, and exhausting one's loyalty, one may engage in worldly affairs; however, one cannot harbor worldly intentions."
Ānanda said: “What,
O God among Gods, are worldly matters and worldly intentions?”
The Buddha said:

"As a disciple of the Buddha, one may engage in the business of trade for profit, provided that one uses level measures and straight rulers without deceiving the people, acts in accordance with reason, and does not contravene the natural order."
Matters such as funerals, moving residence, marriage, and betrothal are worldly affairs.

One who holds worldly views, though claiming to be a disciple of the Buddha, must not practice divination, summon spirits, use talismans or incantations, perform rites to suppress anomalies, conduct ancestral sacrifices, or offer exorcisms; nor should they select auspicious seasons or dates.
One who has received the five precepts of the Buddha is a person of merit; whatever they undertake, they should inform the Triple Gem.
The protection of the Way is powerful, such that even the devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits will all revere and submit to them.
When precepts are honored, one is revered; there is no destination where one will not encounter good fortune. How could there be any prohibitions or things deemed inauspicious!

"Those who do not understand create their own insults; good and evil deeds arise from the mind itself. Calamity and blessing depend on the person, like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound."
The virtue of their preceptual conduct accords with nature; they are protected by the various devas, and their vows never fail. They move the ten directions and share in the merit of the heavens;
their achievements are so lofty that all the sages offer praise, and they are difficult to measure!

"The wise man who understands destiny remains upright throughout his life and does not deviate from the path; by acting in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, he may attain the way to transcend the world.
Having heard what the Buddha said, Ānanda adjusted his *kāṣāya* robe, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, and said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"

We are fortunate to have encountered the Tathāgata, whose universal kindness and compassion are great; he takes pity on all beings, acting as a field of merit for us so that we may be liberated from suffering.
The Buddha said:
“Those who reach the state of perfect truth and possess faith are few; this world abounds in evil, and the mutual cursing among sentient beings is truly pitiable!
If there are those with faith, perhaps only one or two—how can it be that the world is so evil and degenerate to such an extent!”
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the sutras and the Dharma will gradually decline and eventually perish! Alas!
How painful!
"On whom shall we rely?
Ānanda shed tears and, on account of these matters, spoke thus:
"The Buddha is the protector of the three realms; his grace is vast and his compassion universal."
In this degenerate age, it is difficult to see a Buddha; likewise, it is hard to encounter the Dharma.
How painful it is for those who do not recognize it—blind and blind, they cannot distinguish the true.
How painful it is that things have come to such a pass; it is sin that causes them to be thus.
Those who possess the merit of past blessings, whether they be one or two, will see the scriptural teachings gradually vanish; upon what shall we then rely?
The Buddha’s grace is not small, yet sin arises from sentient beings.
The Dharma drum resounds throughout the three thousandfold world; how could one not hear it?
The age is turbid and full of evil people; with inverted views, they fall into perversity.
They flatter and slander the Sages, using crooked seduction to destroy one another.
Lacking faith that there is a Buddha in the world, claiming that the Buddha is not the Great Way,
and asserting that he is a mere human or a non-human, one creates the root of manifold transgressions for oneself.
When life ends, one goes to the Avīci Hell, where swords and blades dismember the physical body.
The hungry ghosts delight in slaughter; boiling cauldrons surge within them.
Those who indulge in lust embrace copper pillars, as great fires consume them.
Those who slander pure and noble sages have their tongues pulled out with iron hooks.
Drinking wine to the point of disorder and lacking propriety, one becomes deluded and loses the way of humanity;
upon death, one enters hell, where molten copper is poured into one's mouth,
encountering manifold perils and dangers, with agonizing pain beyond description.
If one is reborn as a human, one will be among those who are lowly and poor;
by refraining from killing, one attains long life, remains free from illness, and is always healthy and strong;
by refraining from stealing, one becomes greatly wealthy in the future, with money and goods always in abundance.
Abstaining from lust brings purity of fragrance;
the body becomes fresh and sweetly scented, its radiance always brilliant and majestic, and one shall become a Heavenly King above.
Through sincerity and freedom from deceit, one will be honored and supported by the multitude.
Not understanding now, one will later attain clarity; this is what is revered by Virtuous Wisdom.
The five blessings transcend the mundane and emerge from the Dharma;
among gods and humans, one shares their kind, yet the births [of merit] are hundreds of millions of times greater, for the True Truth is most clearly manifest.
In the final age, there will be many evil people, Who lack faith and are full of doubt;
Foolish and ignorant, they cannot distinguish the Path. Their sins being deep, they shall soon reach the dark realm;
Obstructing the sages and slandering the Perfectly Awakened One, They die and enter the Great Iron City.
The conscious spirit dwells within, with an iron wheel upon its head.
Seeking death, it finds no death; in an instant its form is transformed.
Spears and halberds pierce it through, and its body is constantly mangled and severed.
How lamentable it is that the world is thus: turning their backs on the Right, they believe in ghosts and spirits;
they delight in divination and inquiry, and their sacrifices are injurious and unkind.
Upon death they fall into the eighteen hells, passing through the Black Rope Hell.
The eight difficulties constitute the boundary of the world; it is difficult to regain a human body.

Even when one has attained human status, there are those who are barbarians lacking in righteousness and principle, or those who are dull-witted and devoid of intelligence, or those who are lame, crippled, or mute and unable to speak.
In a state of dim confusion, they do not understand the nature of things; driven by mutual hatred, they are bound and entangled.
Turning and twisting, they gather in great throngs, taking on the forms of birds, beasts, and domestic animals.
They are slaughtered by men, their skins flayed and their throats slit open.
Returning to settle old grudges, Giving one's own flesh back to others—
Such lack of principle leads to the evil realms, Where seeking liberation is exceedingly difficult.
Since a human body is so hard to obtain, And the Buddha’s sutras are so hard to hear,
The World-Honored One is the Benefactor of the Multitudes, the uniquely honored one within the three realms;
he spreads the nectar-like Dharma, causing all people to practice it universally.
How compassionate! Having already attained wisdom, he takes pity on all living beings.
When the opening words reveal the true path, the wise immediately cross over suffering.
The person of merit moves ever toward it; seeing the Truth and training, they achieve realization.
Taking refuge in the Great Field of Protection, they plant seeds in the ground of immortality.
There is no benevolence greater than this; the World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma.
May all people be enabled to drink the nectar of immortality, reach the other shore by means of the boat of wisdom, and be led across the great trichiliocosm by the gong of the Dharma.
"That self and that [other] are not two; may you resolve upon the unsurpassed truth.

When Ānanda had spoken thus, the great assembly in the gathering attained faith and understanding. The sound of this nectar-like voice of the great armor of saṃnāha perfumed the three thousandfold world-system.

Having attained deliverance from this, they were revealed to the stages of the Path; for them, he served as a bridge. The king, his ministers and subjects, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, hearing what was recorded in the sutra and spoken by Ānanda, were both sorrowful and joyful. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and paid homage to Ānanda, then received his instructions and departed.
The Sūtra on Ānanda’s Discernment Spoken by the Buddha.
